title: "Binary outcomes"
subtitle: "Proportions, linear probability models and logistic regression"
bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib]
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/housing/_tools.R")

audit <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
analysts <- readr::read_csv("../cases/housing/data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Fixed decimals and a true minus sign, for every number on the page
fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(x, d), "%")
pe <- \(p) dplyr::case_when(p < 0.0001 ~ "p < 0.0001", p < 0.001 ~ paste("p =", fmt(p, 4)),
                     .default = paste("p =", fmt(p, 3)))
an <- \(id, col) analysts[[col]][analysts$id == id]
logit_or <- curve |> datawizard::data_filter(model == "logit") |> datawizard::data_modify(or = exp(coef))

# The EU-frames part of the page (section 9) reads the aggregate tables that
# companion/_model-outputs/fit_items_glm.R wrote from the respondent file;
# nothing of it is refitted here.
prev  <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/items_glm_prevalence.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
coefs <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/items_glm_coefficients.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ame_items <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/items_glm_ame.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
inter <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/items_glm_interaction.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
rnd_file <- "_model-outputs/items_glm_random.csv"
rnd <- if (file.exists(rnd_file)) readr::read_csv(rnd_file, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL

pct_share <- \(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- \(x, d = 3) gsub("-", "−", formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f"), fixed = TRUE)
pv  <- \(it, by, grp) prev$share[prev$item == it & prev$by == by & prev$group == grp]
co  <- \(it, link, term, what = "estimate", vc = "conventional")
  coefs[[what]][coefs$item == it & coefs$link == link & coefs$term == term & coefs$vcov == vc]
am  <- \(it, link, contrast) ame_items$estimate[ame_items$item == it & ame_items$link == link & ame_items$contrast == contrast]
n_resp <- prev$n[prev$item == "it9" & prev$by == "year"] |> sum()
```

This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) works on three cases. Sections 1 to 7 use the housing-audit case, whose outcome is a single yes or no for every email. Section 8 uses the cohabitation case, in which the outcome is asked once for every month of a union and is rare in any one month, and section 9 the EU-frames case, in which respondents are grouped in country-years and the clustering, the link and a country-level predictor become part of the model.

Sections 1 to 7 fit the models that the course uses for a yes-or-no outcome, on the outcome of the housing-audit claim: whether a reply from a housing authority opened with the name of the person who wrote to it. The housing-audit case comes from a field experiment by the original authors (OAs), who emailed public housing authorities from six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], and the [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd) describes it. The module starts from a table of counts and builds up to the logistic regression of the paper, so that each step can be checked against the one before it. Every number is computed when the page is built, from the files of the course in `cases/housing/data/`, and the code is shown. The estimator of the course, `fit_spec()` in `R/housing/_tools.R`, does the same arithmetic for every specification of the curve.

## 1. A yes-or-no outcome {#sec-outcome}

A reply either opened with the name of the sender or it did not, so the outcome takes the values 1 and 0, and its mean in a group of replies is the share that opened with the name. Every model on this page describes that share, the probability of a 1, and how it differs between emails with Hispanic and with white names. The rows are the replies to those two groups of names that carry a greeting code, and `spec_frame()` from the estimator of the course selects them, with the outcome as `y` and the Hispanic names coded 1 in `hisp`.

```{r}
#| label: table
frame <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
counts <- table(hispanic = frame$hisp, named = frame$y)  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() and prop.test() take a table
counts
shares <- frame |> dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), named = sum(y), share = mean(y), .by = hisp) |> dplyr::arrange(hisp)
shares
```

Of the `r shares$n[1]` coded replies to white names, `r shares$named[1]` opened with the name, `r pct(100 * shares$share[1])`, against `r shares$named[2]` of the `r shares$n[2]` replies to Hispanic names, `r pct(100 * shares$share[2])`. Everything that follows is a way of describing the difference between those two shares, and of saying how far it could have arisen by chance.

## 2. The difference in proportions {#sec-difference}

The plainest summary is the difference between the two shares, `r fmt(100 * diff(shares$share), 2)` percentage points, which is also the scale on which the abstract of the paper states the claim. Its standard error follows from the variance of a 0/1 variable, which is $p(1 - p)$ for a share $p$, so that each group contributes its own variance divided by its size.

```{r}
#| label: difference
p1 <- shares$share[2]
p0 <- shares$share[1]
n1 <- shares$n[2]
n0 <- shares$n[1]
gap <- p1 - p0
se_gap <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
round(100 * c(gap = gap, se = se_gap, lower = gap - 1.96 * se_gap, upper = gap + 1.96 * se_gap), 2)
```

The gap of `r fmt(100 * gap, 2)` points has a standard error of `r fmt(100 * se_gap, 2)` points and a 95% confidence interval from `r fmt(100 * (gap - 1.96 * se_gap))` to `r fmt(100 * (gap + 1.96 * se_gap))`.

The classical test of the same difference is the $\chi^2$ test of the two-by-two table, which R offers as `chisq.test()` and, in the form of a test of two proportions, as `prop.test()`. Both compare the observed counts with the counts expected if the two groups shared one share of named greetings. Without a correction the $\chi^2$ statistic is exactly the square of the z of the two proportions, computed with that shared share in its standard error.

```{r}
#| label: chisq
pooled <- mean(frame$y)
z_pooled <- gap / sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n0))
c(z_squared = z_pooled^2,
  chisq_uncorrected = unname(chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)$statistic),
  chisq_corrected = unname(chisq.test(counts)$statistic),
  prop_test = unname(prop.test(counts[, 2:1])$statistic)) |>
  round(3)
```

The last two numbers differ from the first two because `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply the continuity correction to a two-by-two table unless they are told otherwise. The correction, due to Yates, shrinks each difference between an observed and an expected count by half a unit before it is squared, which makes the test a little more conservative. It matters for the reproduction in Task 3. Analyst 8PTRZ compared the Hispanic names with all other names among the replies and recorded $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(an("8PTRZ", "statistic_recorded"), 3)`, the corrected value, and analyst 25N5D recorded the corrected `prop.test()` statistic of `r fmt(an("25N5D", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` for the comparison among all delivered emails.

```{r}
#| label: analysts-chisq
frame_8ptrz <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "nonhispanic", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
frame_25n5d <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "not_named")
tab_8ptrz <- table(frame_8ptrz$hisp, frame_8ptrz$y)  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() takes a table
c(`8PTRZ` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic),
  `8PTRZ, uncorrected` = unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic),
  `25N5D` = unname(prop.test(table(frame_25n5d$hisp, frame_25n5d$y)[, 2:1])$statistic)) |>  # r-style: keep – prop.test() takes a table
  round(3)
```

Both recorded values come out exactly, and without the correction the statistic of 8PTRZ would have been `r fmt(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic, 2)`. A reproduction depends on the defaults of the software as well as on the data and the model. The test of a table is a check on the curve of the claim, which tests every specification by its model instead, because a model can carry covariates and a table cannot.

## 3. The linear probability model {#sec-lpm}

A linear regression of the 0/1 outcome on the 0/1 indicator of the Hispanic names is called a linear probability model. With a single binary predictor it reproduces the table exactly: the intercept is the share among the white names and the coefficient is the difference in proportions.

```{r}
#| label: lpm
lpm <- lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame)
round(coef(lpm), 4)
# classical errors; HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from the sandwich
# package (Zeileis 2004, Journal of Statistical Software); and the standard
# error of the difference between two means computed group by group, from the
# Welch t-test
se <- c(classical = sqrt(vcov(lpm)["hisp", "hisp"]),
        hc2 = sqrt(sandwich::vcovHC(lpm, type = "HC2")["hisp", "hisp"]),
        two_sample = t.test(y ~ hisp, data = frame)$stderr)
round(100 * se, 4)
```

The classical formula for the standard error of a linear regression assumes that the outcome varies equally in both groups, which a 0/1 outcome cannot do unless the two shares are equal or add up to one, since its variance is $p(1 - p)$. The HC2 standard error, one of the heteroskedasticity-consistent errors that allow the variance to differ between observations, drops that assumption, and with one binary predictor it equals the standard error of a difference between two means computed group by group, the formula that is used for comparing two randomised groups. The course computes it with `vcovHC()` from the sandwich package, which the estimator of the course reaches through `parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2")`, and the `estimatr` package gives the same number with `lm_robust(y ~ hisp, se_type = "HC2")`. Here the classical and the HC2 errors differ by only `r fmt(100 * abs(se[["classical"]] - se[["hc2"]]), 3)` points, because the two groups are of similar size and the two shares not far apart, but the HC2 error is the one that stays right when they are not.

The linear probability model has a well-known fault, which shows once covariates enter: a straight line has no floor or ceiling, so it can predict a share below 0 or above 1. With the covariates of the curve, which are a handful of categories, the predictions stay well inside that range on these data.

```{r}
#| label: lpm-range
lpm_adjusted <- lm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third + black_third + hispanic_third,
                   data = frame)
round(range(fitted(lpm_adjusted)), 3)
```

In an experiment with a binary treatment the linear probability model has a second virtue. Its coefficient is the difference in proportions, the quantity that the claim names, whether or not covariates are added, and on this curve the covariates move it by less than the width of its standard error. That is why the reference specification of the curve is a linear probability model without covariates.

## 4. Logistic regression {#sec-logit}

The model of the paper is a logistic regression, which models the log of the odds of a greeting, $\log(p / (1 - p))$, a transformation of the share that runs over the whole real line and so keeps every prediction between 0 and 1. Its coefficients are differences in log odds.

```{r}
#| label: logit
logit <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = frame)
round(coef(logit), 4)
round(exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]]), 3)
predicted <- predict(logit, newdata = tibble::tibble(hisp = c(0, 1)), type = "response")
round(100 * predicted, 2)
```

The coefficient of the Hispanic names is `r fmt(coef(logit)[["hisp"]], 3)`, close to the −0.82 of the paper, whose model also carried the community covariates and the hard-to-find address and fitted all three groups of names at once. Exponentiated, it is an odds ratio of `r fmt(exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]]), 3)`: the odds that a reply to a Hispanic name opened with the name were `r fmt(exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]]), 2)` times the odds for a white name. Without covariates the model reproduces the two observed shares exactly, `r pct(100 * predicted[1])` and `r pct(100 * predicted[2])`, so their difference is again the gap of `r fmt(100 * gap, 2)` points.

The OAs, EWFMI and P9W8Y fitted the three groups in one model. The OAs took the white names as the base category and EWFMI the Hispanic names, which is why the z of that analyst is positive; P9W8Y reported an omnibus test, which does not depend on the base. Without covariates the three-group model gives exactly the same coefficient for the Hispanic names as the two-group model, since each coefficient compares one group with the base and the third group adds nothing to that comparison.

```{r}
#| label: three-group
three <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, !is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = relevel(factor(group), ref = "white"))
round(coef(glm(named ~ group, family = binomial(), data = three)), 4)
```

With covariates the two differ a little, because the emails with Black names then help to estimate the covariates, and the specification menu keeps the three-group model as a check of the two-group fit.

## 5. Odds ratios and percentage points {#sec-scales}

Odds ratios are the conventional way of reporting a logistic regression, and they are exact and portable, but they are hard to picture, because the same odds ratio means very different changes in probability at different starting points. The chunk below applies the odds ratio of the data to four shares of named greetings for the white names.

```{r}
#| label: or-scale
odds_ratio <- exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]])
base <- c(0.20, 0.50, 0.61, 0.90)
odds_hisp <- odds_ratio * base / (1 - base)
or_gaps <- 100 * (odds_hisp / (1 + odds_hisp) - base)
round(or_gaps, 1)
```

The odds ratio of `r fmt(odds_ratio, 3)` turns a share of 61% into a gap of `r fmt(or_gaps[3])` points, but a share of 20% into a gap of `r fmt(or_gaps[1])` points and a share of 90% into one of `r fmt(or_gaps[4])`.

The claim, in the abstract, states the gap in percentage points, and so does every point of the curve. A logistic regression reports its result on that scale through an average marginal effect, the difference in the predicted probability of a greeting between a Hispanic and a white name, computed for every analysed email as it is and averaged. The estimator of the course computes it with `avg_comparisons()` from the marginaleffects package, which sets the indicator of the Hispanic names to 1 and then to 0 in every row, predicts the probability of a greeting each time, and averages the difference; `avg_predictions()` shows the two averages from which the difference is taken. One detail of that package catches people out: it refuses a data column called `group`, so the model is fitted on the model columns alone.

```{r}
#| label: ame
model_cols <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("y", "hisp", "hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(dplyr::everything(), \(x) !is.na(x)))
logit_adjusted <- glm(y ~ hisp + hard_email + pop_third + poverty_third + black_third + hispanic_third,
                      family = binomial(), data = model_cols)
# the average predicted probability with every email signed by a white name and
# by a Hispanic one, and their difference with its delta-method standard error
marginaleffects::avg_predictions(logit_adjusted, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(logit_adjusted, variables = "hisp")
round(100 * c(ame = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error), 3)
```

The difference between the two average predictions is the average marginal effect. Across the `r nrow(logit_or)` logistic specifications of the curve the odds ratio runs from `r fmt(min(logit_or$or), 3)` to `r fmt(max(logit_or$or), 3)`, and the average marginal effect from `r fmt(min(logit_or$b_pp))` to `r fmt(max(logit_or$b_pp))` points. A related rule bounds the size of a logistic coefficient on the probability scale. The slope of the logistic curve is steepest, at one quarter, where the probability is one half, so a coefficient $b$ moves a probability by at most $b/4$. The SCORE replication found a coefficient of 0.098 for its Hispanic names, which is therefore a gap of at most `r fmt(100 * 0.098 / 4, 2)` points, in their favour.

## 6. Odds ratios and covariates {#sec-collapsibility}

In a randomised experiment, adding a covariate that predicts the outcome does not change what a difference in proportions estimates, because the covariate is unrelated to the treatment. It does change what an odds ratio estimates, even with no confounding at all. The odds ratio is said to be non-collapsible: an odds ratio that holds within each group of a covariate does not hold for the groups taken together. The arithmetic shows why. Suppose the authorities were of two kinds, equally many of each, and that white names were greeted by name 85% of the time by one kind and 35% of the time by the other, about the 61% of the data on average. Let the Hispanic names multiply the odds of a greeting by the odds ratio of the data in both kinds of authority.

```{r}
#| label: non-collapsible
white_by_kind <- c(0.85, 0.35)
hisp_odds <- odds_ratio * white_by_kind / (1 - white_by_kind)
hisp_by_kind <- hisp_odds / (1 + hisp_odds)
white_all <- mean(white_by_kind)
hisp_all <- mean(hisp_by_kind)
round(c(or_within = odds_ratio,
        or_all = (hisp_all / (1 - hisp_all)) / (white_all / (1 - white_all)),
        gap_kind_1 = 100 * (hisp_by_kind[1] - white_by_kind[1]),
        gap_kind_2 = 100 * (hisp_by_kind[2] - white_by_kind[2]),
        gap_all = 100 * (hisp_all - white_all)), 3)
```

Within each kind of authority the odds ratio is `r fmt(odds_ratio, 3)`, but for all authorities together it is `r fmt((hisp_all / (1 - hisp_all)) / (white_all / (1 - white_all)), 3)`, closer to 1, although nothing is confounded and the names were assigned at random. The gaps in percentage points behave as one would hope: the gap for all authorities, `r fmt(100 * (hisp_all - white_all))` points, is the average of the gaps within the two kinds. A logistic regression that adjusts for the kind of authority would report an odds ratio of `r fmt(odds_ratio, 3)` and one that does not would report `r fmt((hisp_all / (1 - hisp_all)) / (white_all / (1 - white_all)), 3)`, and both would be right about different quantities, the odds ratio within a kind of authority and the odds ratio over all of them.

On the housing-audit data the covariates predict the greeting only weakly, so the effect is small and mixes with the chance differences between the groups. On the `r nrow(model_cols)` replies that carry every covariate, the adjusted model gives an odds ratio of `r fmt(exp(coef(logit_adjusted)[["hisp"]]), 3)` against `r fmt(exp(coef(glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = model_cols))[["hisp"]]), 3)` without covariates, and an average marginal effect of `r fmt(100 * ame$estimate)` against `r fmt(100 * marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = model_cols), variables = "hisp")$estimate)` points. Both shifts come mainly from small imbalances in the covariates between the groups, which adjustment corrects, and not from non-collapsibility. The principle matters for comparing results. An odds ratio from a model with covariates and one from a model without them are not estimates of the same quantity, so two analysts who report odds ratios from different models can differ for that reason alone, which is one reason why the course reports every logistic specification as an average marginal effect in points.

## 7. The methods side by side {#sec-side-by-side}

Every method on this page can be applied to the one comparison of the reference specification, Hispanic against white names among the `r nrow(frame)` coded replies, and @tbl-side-by-side sets them in one table.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-side-by-side
#| tbl-cap: "One comparison, Hispanic against white names among the coded replies, reported by each method of the page: the estimate on its own scale, its standard error, the test statistic and the two-sided p-value. The randomisation p-value is stored in the curve file. Sources: `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv`, `cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv`."
#| code-fold: true
# each model reported by parameters (classical, HC2 and Wald z), the average
# marginal effect by marginaleffects
lpm_classical <- parameters::model_parameters(lpm) |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
lpm_hc2 <- parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2") |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
logit_row <- parameters::model_parameters(logit) |> datawizard::data_filter(Parameter == "hisp")
logit_z <- logit_row$z
# marginaleffects refuses a data column called group, so the logit is refitted
# on the model columns alone for it
logit_ame <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(),
                 data = datawizard::data_select(frame, select = c("y", "hisp"))) |>
  marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(variables = "hisp")
chi_plain <- chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)
chi_yates <- chisq.test(counts)
ref_spec <- curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
all_p <- c(2 * pnorm(-abs(gap / se_gap)), chi_plain$p.value, chi_yates$p.value,
           lpm_hc2$p, logit_row$p, ref_spec$p_ri)
tibble::tribble(
  ~Method, ~Estimate, ~SE, ~Statistic, ~p,
  "Difference in proportions", fmt(100 * gap, 2), fmt(100 * se_gap, 2),
    paste("z =", fmt(gap / se_gap, 2)), pe(2 * pnorm(-abs(gap / se_gap))),
  "χ<sup>2</sup> test, uncorrected", "", "", paste("χ<sup>2</sup> =", fmt(chi_plain$statistic, 2)),
    pe(chi_plain$p.value),
  "χ<sup>2</sup> test, with the continuity correction", "", "",
    paste("χ<sup>2</sup> =", fmt(chi_yates$statistic, 2)), pe(chi_yates$p.value),
  "Linear probability model, classical errors", fmt(100 * lpm_classical$Coefficient, 2),
    fmt(100 * lpm_classical$SE, 2), paste("t =", fmt(lpm_classical$t, 2)), pe(lpm_classical$p),
  "Linear probability model, HC2 errors", fmt(100 * lpm_hc2$Coefficient, 2),
    fmt(100 * lpm_hc2$SE, 2), paste("t =", fmt(lpm_hc2$t, 2)), pe(lpm_hc2$p),
  "Logistic regression, coefficient", fmt(logit_row$Coefficient, 3), fmt(logit_row$SE, 3),
    paste("z =", fmt(logit_z, 3)), pe(logit_row$p),
  "Logistic regression, average marginal effect", fmt(100 * logit_ame$estimate, 2),
    fmt(100 * logit_ame$std.error, 2), "", "",
  "Randomisation test", "", "", "", paste("p =", fmt(ref_spec$p_ri, 4))
) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

Every method finds the same gap, or a statistic that tests it, and the largest p-value in the table is `r fmt(max(all_p), 4)`, that of the randomisation test, which cannot go lower with 1,999 reshuffles. The z of the logistic coefficient, `r fmt(logit_z, 3)`, is the value that analyst UYV3F recorded. The methods differ in what they can carry and in the scale on which they report. A table test carries no covariates, a linear probability model reports in points and a logistic regression in log odds unless it is converted. They also differ in the statistic that they hand on to anyone who converts results to a common scale, which is why the same gap became different correlations in Multi100, as the [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-scale) shows.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Change the two shares of the arithmetic in section 6 to 0.65 and 0.55, which predict the greeting much more weakly, and rerun the chunk. How far does the odds ratio for all authorities now move from the odds ratio within them? Then go back to 0.85 and 0.35 and replace the odds ratio of the data with 1, the case where the names make no difference: does the odds ratio for all authorities still move?
:::

## 8. The cohabitation case {#sec-cohabitation}

::: {.callout-note}
If you are working through the cohabitation case, read this section after Task 3 of the case, which asks you to look at the data for yourself first.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup-cohabitation
#| include: false
# section 8: the person-months of the cohabitation case, from the files of the
# course rebuild of the unions; the objects of the section carry the prefix
# co_. The case numbers, strata and clusters are codes, so readr reads them as
# text.
co_types <- readr::cols(caseid = readr::col_character(), stratum = readr::col_character(),
                        psu = readr::col_character())
co_curve <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
co_options <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/display_options.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
# the reference settings of the curve with the model left free
co_ref <- co_curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cohorts == "paper", horizon == "five_years", adjust == "composition",
                          weights == "weighted", time == "linear")
co_b <- stats::setNames(co_ref$b, co_ref$model)
```

The cohabitation case takes its claim from a study in *Demography* by the original authors (OAs) of that case, and in this section OAs refers to them: American "cohabitors have increasingly become less likely to progress to marriage" [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion]. The study compares the first cohabitations that came before any marriage, begun in 1990–1995 among the women interviewed by the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) in 1995 and begun in 2005–2010 among the women interviewed in 2006–2010, and the [case study](../cases/cohabitation/index.qmd) describes it. The outcome is again yes or no, whether a cohabiting couple married, but it differs from the greeting of the housing-audit case in one respect that changes the model. A union may have been observed for a month or for five years before the interview, and a couple observed for longer has had more time to marry, so a comparison of the shares that had married by the interview mixes the chance of marrying with the time for which each union was observed. Event-history analysis asks instead, once for every month, whether the couple married in that month, given that they were still together when it began. One union becomes many yes-or-no outcomes, almost all of them no. The [event-history module](event-history.qmd) builds the method from the beginning, and this section sets it beside the models of sections 1 to 7 as a model for a binary outcome. Every number is computed when the page is built from the person-month file of the course rebuild of the unions, `cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months.csv`.

### 8.1 One row per month {#sec-person-months}

The person-month file has one row for every month in which a union could have ended, from the month in which the couple moved in to the month in which they married, separated or, for a union still intact, the woman was interviewed. The outcome of the union is recorded in its last row, and every earlier row is a month in which nothing happened. `marry` is 1 in a month in which the couple married and 0 otherwise, so a month in which they separated is a 0 after which the union leaves the data, because a separated couple can no longer marry each other.

```{r}
#| label: person-months
co_months <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = co_types) |>
  # the unions of the paper: in 2006-2010 only those begun from 2005
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle == "1995" | from_2005) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(marry = as.integer(y == "marriage"), age2 = age_start^2,
                          race = factor(race, c("white", "black", "hispanic", "other")),
                          educ = factor(educ, c("college", "some_college", "hs", "less_hs")),
                          w = weight / mean(weight), keep = TRUE)

# a union of 1995 that became a marriage in its fourth month
co_months |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle == "1995") |>
  dplyr::filter(caseid == dplyr::first(caseid[y == "marriage" & month == 4])) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("cycle", "caseid", "month", "y", "marry"))
```

The `r format(nrow(co_months), big.mark = ",")` person-months of the paper belong to `r format(dplyr::n_distinct(paste(co_months$cycle, co_months$caseid)), big.mark = ",")` unions, and `r sum(co_months$marry)` of them record a marriage, `r pct(100 * mean(co_months$marry))` of the rows. That is the first difference from the housing-audit case, in which `r pct(100 * mean(frame$y))` of the coded replies to white and Hispanic names opened with the name. The second is that the rows are not independent observations. The months of one union belong to one couple, and the women were sampled in clusters within strata, so the errors of every model below follow the design of the two surveys, as the [weights module](weighting.qmd#sec-cohabitation) explains.

### 8.2 The discrete-time logit {#sec-discrete-logit}

A logistic regression of `marry` on the person-months is the simplest discrete-time event-history model. It models the log odds that a couple married in a month, given that they were still together at its start, with the later cohort (`later`, 1 for the unions of 2005–2010), the months since the couple moved in, and the controls of the reference specification of the curve: the age at the start and its square, race-ethnicity and education. The fit below uses the survey weights and declares the design of the surveys on every one of their clusters before keeping the analysed months, which is how the estimator of the case does it.

```{r}
#| label: discrete-logit
# every stratum and cluster of the two surveys, with no months of their own
co_clusters <- readr::read_csv("../cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                               col_types = co_types) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle %in% c("1995", "2006-10")) |>
  dplyr::distinct(stratum, psu) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(w = 1, keep = FALSE)
co_design <- survey::svydesign(ids = ~psu, strata = ~stratum, weights = ~w, nest = TRUE,
                               data = dplyr::bind_rows(co_months, co_clusters)) |>
  subset(keep)  # r-style: keep – the subset method of a survey design keeps the strata of the full design
# quasibinomial() gives the coefficients of binomial() without its warning
# about weights that are not whole numbers
co_logit <- survey::svyglm(marry ~ later + month + age_start + age2 + race + educ,
                           design = co_design, family = stats::quasibinomial())
parameters::model_parameters(co_logit, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(Parameter %in% c("later", "month"))
```

```{r}
#| label: discrete-logit-check
#| include: false
# the same fit as the logit of the curve at the reference settings
# (to 1e-5: the estimator of the case iterates to a stricter criterion)
stopifnot(abs(stats::coef(co_logit)[["later"]] - co_b[["logit"]]) < 1e-5)
```

The coefficient of the later cohort is `r fmt(stats::coef(co_logit)[["later"]], 3)`, an odds ratio of `r fmt(exp(stats::coef(co_logit)[["later"]]), 3)`: in a given month of the union, the odds that a couple of 2005–2010 married were less than half the odds for a couple of 1990–1995 of the same age at the start, race-ethnicity and education. The months since the start enter as a straight line on the log-odds scale, the baseline of the reference specification, and the [event-history module](event-history.qmd#sec-logit) sets it beside other baselines. The fit is the logit of the curve of the case at its reference settings, the same coefficient to five decimals.

### 8.3 A rare outcome {#sec-rare}

The probability scale of section 5 applies here as well. `avg_predictions()` gives the average monthly chance of marrying with every union set to the earlier cohort and then to the later one, each union keeping its own months, age, race-ethnicity and education, averaged with the survey weights; `avg_comparisons()` gives their difference, the average marginal effect, and their ratio.

```{r}
#| label: rare-outcome
co_pred <- marginaleffects::avg_predictions(co_logit, variables = "later", wts = "(weights)")
co_pred
co_ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(co_logit, variables = "later", wts = "(weights)")
co_ratio <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(co_logit, variables = "later", wts = "(weights)",
                                             comparison = "ratioavg")
round(c(ame_points = 100 * co_ame$estimate, se_points = 100 * co_ame$std.error,
        ratio_of_chances = co_ratio$estimate, odds_ratio = exp(stats::coef(co_logit)[["later"]])), 3)
```

The average monthly chance of marrying falls by `r fmt(100 * abs(co_ame$estimate), 2)` percentage points, from `r pct(100 * co_pred$estimate[co_pred$later == 0], 2)` to `r pct(100 * co_pred$estimate[co_pred$later == 1], 2)` a month, and the ratio of the two chances is `r fmt(co_ratio$estimate, 3)`, almost the odds ratio of `r fmt(exp(stats::coef(co_logit)[["later"]]), 3)`. When a chance $p$ is small, the odds $p / (1 - p)$ are almost $p$, so a ratio of odds is almost a ratio of chances. In the housing-audit case the same two numbers part: the odds ratio of the greeting was `r fmt(exp(coef(logit)[["hisp"]]), 3)`, while the share of replies that opened with the name was `r fmt(shares$share[2] / shares$share[1], 3)` times as large for Hispanic as for white names. The warnings of sections 5 and 6, that an odds ratio is hard to picture and changes when a covariate is added, therefore bite hardest when the outcome is common, and they matter far less when it is rare.

The choice of link matters little for the same reason. At the reference settings the curve gives `r fmt(co_b[["logit"]], 3)` for the logit, `r fmt(co_b[["cloglog"]], 3)` for the complementary log-log model and `r fmt(co_b[["mlogit"]], 3)` for the multinomial logit of the paper. The complementary log-log coefficient is the log of a ratio of monthly rates, from the version of the proportional hazards model for time that is measured in whole months, and the multinomial logit models marriage and separation together, each against staying together. With a monthly chance of a few per cent the three coefficients nearly coincide, and the curve keeps all three.

A rare outcome also changes what a correlation can show. At the reference settings the partial correlation of the later cohort with marrying in the month, by the conversion rule of Multi100, is `r fmt(co_ref$r[co_ref$model == "logit"], 3)`, although the monthly chance halved. Almost every row is a 0, and a correlation over person-months stays small whatever the size of the change. A correlation is therefore a poor common scale for results on rare outcomes, which matters wherever the results of several analysts are converted to one scale, as the [case study of the housing-audit case](../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-scale) shows for the greeting.

### 8.4 The linear probability model near zero {#sec-lpm-floor}

The linear probability model of section 3 gives the difference in the monthly chance directly, as its coefficient, and on the person-months its fault, a straight line without floor or ceiling, becomes visible.

```{r}
#| label: lpm-floor
co_lpm <- stats::lm(marry ~ later + month + age_start + age2 + race + educ, data = co_months, weights = w)
round(100 * c(later = stats::coef(co_lpm)[["later"]], range(stats::fitted(co_lpm))), 2)
round(100 * mean(stats::fitted(co_lpm) < 0), 1)
```

Its coefficient, `r fmt(100 * stats::coef(co_lpm)[["later"]], 2)` points a month, is almost the average marginal effect of the logit, `r fmt(100 * co_ame$estimate, 2)`, and the estimator of the case gives `r fmt(100 * co_options$b[co_options$option == "lpm"], 2)` with the design of the surveys. Its predictions run from `r pct(100 * min(stats::fitted(co_lpm)), 2)` to `r pct(100 * max(stats::fitted(co_lpm)), 2)`, and `r pct(100 * mean(stats::fitted(co_lpm) < 0))` of the months receive a negative chance of marrying, which no month can have. In the housing-audit case the predictions stayed well inside the range from 0 to 1, because the shares were far from both ends. The linear probability model is a fair check of the size of a change in a rare outcome and a poor model of the outcome itself, and the menu of the case keeps it off the curve as a check, because its coefficient is on another scale from the log ratios of the curve.

## 9. The EU-frames case {#sec-eu-frames}

The housing-audit data are a single experiment, in which every email is independent of every other, and in the cohabitation case the dependence between the months of a union and between the women of a sampled cluster is handled by the design of the survey. In the EU-frames case respondents are grouped in country-years that differ in their economic conditions, so the grouping is part of the question, and this section fits the models of the page to a yes-or-no answer with that grouping in view. The outcome is the simplest one in that case: one item of the question that asks what the European Union means to the respondent personally. Every framing scale on the specification menu is built from thirteen such items, so an item is the rung of the data ladder below every scale, and a model for one item is the building block under everything that the [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd) fits to the scales and that the [items module](measurement.qmd) says about how they hang together. The page follows two items: "Unemployment", the answer that shares its content with the predictor of the whole case, and "Peace", the most-named positive answer after freedom to travel.

Everything in this section was fitted on the real respondents, the `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` people in the file that the build script of the EU-frames workspace produces from the sixteen GESIS surveys, and written out as the aggregate tables that the page reads; the [respondent codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/eb_respondents_codebook.md) describes the variables. The script that fitted them, `companion/_model-outputs/fit_items_glm.R`, runs on that file, so anyone who has built it can refit every model of the section. Besides sections 1 to 7, it assumes section 2 of the statistics module, on the first linear model.

The section uses a second link besides the logit. The probit models the point on a standard normal distribution below which a share *p* of the area lies, so that a coefficient in a probit model is a difference in standard-normal units, where a logit coefficient is a difference in log-odds. Neither is a probability, and section 9.4 is about getting back to one.

### 9.1 Who names unemployment, and when {#sec-prevalence}

The two items differ in level and in who names them. "Peace" is named by about `r pct_share(mean(prev$share[prev$item == "it1" & prev$by == "year"]))` of respondents across the ten years and "Unemployment" by about `r pct_share(mean(prev$share[prev$item == "it9" & prev$by == "year"]))`, and both move with the education of the respondent, in opposite directions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-prev-edu
#| tbl-cap: "Share of respondents naming each item, by education band. Bands are the published ones, from the age at which full-time education finished."
prev |>
  datawizard::data_filter(by == "education") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(group = factor(group, c("low", "mid", "high"))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("item", "group")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = label, Education = as.character(group), `Named by` = pct_share(share), Respondents = format(n, big.mark = ",")) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

The low-educated name unemployment almost twice as often as the high-educated, `r pct_share(pv("it9", "education", "low"))` against `r pct_share(pv("it9", "education", "high"))`, and the high-educated name peace more often than the low-educated, `r pct_share(pv("it1", "education", "high"))` against `r pct_share(pv("it1", "education", "low"))`. Before any model has been fitted, those two differences are the raw material of the first part of the second hypothesis of the original paper, H2a, that the high-educated frame the EU more positively and less negatively.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prev-year
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Share of respondents naming each item, by fieldwork year, across the twenty-seven member states."
prev |>
  datawizard::data_filter(by == "year") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(year = as.integer(group)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(year, share, colour = label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(Peace = "#0e3b6a", Unemployment = "#96131b"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2004:2013) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(100 * x, "%"), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "named by") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Both items also change over the decade. "Unemployment" falls from `r pct_share(pv("it9", "year", "2004"))` in 2004 to `r pct_share(pv("it9", "year", "2008"))` in 2008, the last year before the crisis reached the labour market, and climbs back to `r pct_share(pv("it9", "year", "2013"))` by 2013. "Peace" declines from `r pct_share(pv("it1", "year", "2004"))` to `r pct_share(pv("it1", "year", "2011"))` in 2011. That the item which names the predictor of the case tracks the predictor so visibly is one reason that the specification menu offers an item set without it.

### 9.2 Logit and probit, side by side {#sec-links}

Both links are fitted with the same predictors: the three education bands, age, sex, the eight occupational groups and the three types of community, which is the respondent-level part of the published models. The coefficients are on different scales and the table shows them next to each other.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-links
#| tbl-cap: "Logit and probit coefficients for naming 'Unemployment', conventional standard errors, selected terms. The reference categories are the lowest education band, men, manual workers and large towns. The last column is the logit coefficient over the probit coefficient."
coefs |>
  datawizard::data_filter(item == "it9", vcov == "conventional",
         term %in% c("edu3mid", "edu3high", "age_c", "female", "sesunemployed", "sesstudent", "sesretired")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("term", "link", "estimate", "se")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = link, values_from = c(estimate, se)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(term = dplyr::recode(term, edu3mid = "education: mid", edu3high = "education: high", age_c = "age (years, centred)",
                       female = "female", sesunemployed = "unemployed", sesstudent = "student", sesretired = "retired"),
         ratio = estimate_logit / estimate_probit) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Term = term, `Logit b` = num(estimate_logit), `(SE)` = num(se_logit),
            `Probit b` = num(estimate_probit), `(SE) ` = num(se_probit), `Logit / probit` = num(ratio, 2)) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

The two links order and sign every coefficient identically, and each logit coefficient is about 1.6 to 1.8 times its probit counterpart, which is the known ratio between the scales of the logistic and the normal distributions. The choice of link therefore changes the units in which the coefficients are expressed, while their signs and their order stay the same. As for their sizes, being in the highest education band rather than the lowest lowers the log-odds of naming unemployment by `r num(abs(co("it9", "logit", "edu3high")))`, which is an odds ratio of `r num(exp(co("it9", "logit", "edu3high")), 2)`, meaning that the odds of naming it are about half those in the lowest band. Being unemployed oneself raises the log-odds by `r num(co("it9", "logit", "sesunemployed"))`, an odds ratio of `r num(exp(co("it9", "logit", "sesunemployed")), 2)`; being a student lowers them by more than being unemployed raises them. Odds ratios are the conventional way of reporting a logit, and they are exact and portable. They are also hard to picture, because a doubling of small odds and a doubling of large odds are very different changes in probability, which is why section 9.4 converts them, as section 5 did for the housing-audit data.

### 9.3 The cluster {#sec-cluster}

The standard errors in the table above assume that the `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` respondents are independent draws. They are not, because they are grouped in 270 country-years, and respondents in the same country-year share a survey, a moment and a labour market. The [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-pooled) makes the same point for the panel; here it is made for a binary outcome, by refitting the logit with standard errors clustered by country-year.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cluster
#| tbl-cap: "The logit for 'Unemployment' under conventional and cluster-robust standard errors (clusters are country-years). The coefficients are identical, and only the standard errors and the z statistics change."
coefs |>
  datawizard::data_filter(item == "it9", link == "logit",
         term %in% c("edu3mid", "edu3high", "age_c", "female", "sesunemployed")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("term", "vcov", "estimate", "se", "z")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(term = dplyr::recode(term, edu3mid = "education: mid", edu3high = "education: high", age_c = "age (years, centred)",
                       female = "female", sesunemployed = "unemployed"),
         vcov = dplyr::if_else(vcov == "conventional", "conventional", "clustered")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = vcov, values_from = c(se, z)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Term = term, b = num(estimate), `SE, conventional` = num(se_conventional), `z` = num(z_conventional, 1),
            `SE, clustered` = num(se_clustered), `z ` = num(z_clustered, 1)) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

The standard error of the high-education coefficient nearly triples once the clustering is admitted, and its z statistic falls from `r num(co("it9", "logit", "edu3high", "z"), 1)` to `r num(co("it9", "logit", "edu3high", "z", "clustered by country-year"), 1)`. No coefficient in the table loses its significance, because the education gap is large and consistent across cells, but the conventional errors overstate the precision by a factor that would lead to a real mistake with a predictor that varies only at the cell level. Section 8.5 shows that predictor. The other way of dealing with the cluster is to model it, with a random intercept for the country-year, and section 9.7 does that.

### 9.4 From coefficients to probabilities {#sec-ame}

A coefficient on the link scale is a change in the log-odds, while the question that a reader usually has is by how many percentage points the probability changes. The average marginal effect gives that figure: for every respondent, the change in predicted probability that the model implies for a change in one variable, averaged over the respondents as they are.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ame
#| tbl-cap: "Average marginal effects on the probability of naming each item, from the logit and from the probit, averaged over a random fifty thousand respondents; standard errors clustered by country-year. Education contrasts are against the lowest band."
ame_items |>
  datawizard::data_modify(term = dplyr::case_when(contrast == "high - low" ~ "education: high vs low",
                          contrast == "mid - low"  ~ "education: mid vs low",
                          term == "female"         ~ "female vs male",
                          TRUE                     ~ "age, per year"),
         item = dplyr::if_else(item == "it9", "Unemployment", "Peace")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("item", "term", "link", "estimate", "se")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = link, values_from = c(estimate, se)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = item, Term = term,
            `Logit, points` = num(100 * estimate_logit, 2), `(SE)` = num(100 * se_logit, 2),
            `Probit, points` = num(100 * estimate_probit, 2), `(SE) ` = num(100 * se_probit, 2)) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

On the probability scale the two links agree to the second decimal, which settles the logit-or-probit question for practical purposes. The differences are those of the prevalence table with the other characteristics taken into account: a high-educated respondent is `r num(100 * abs(am("it9", "logit", "high - low")), 1)` percentage points less likely to name unemployment than a low-educated one of the same age, sex, occupation and community, and `r num(100 * am("it1", "logit", "high - low"), 1)` points more likely to name peace. The [quantitative writing register](../resources.qmd) of the course asks for binary models to be reported this way, in points of probability with the uncertainty estimated by the model, because a difference in points of probability is one that a reader can weigh.

### 9.5 The national unemployment rate on a single item {#sec-macro}

The predictor in the case is the unemployment rate of the country in the survey year, and it can be entered in a model for one item as it is in a model for a scale. Two ways to do it are shown, and they disagree in the way that the panel models of the statistics module disagree. Pooled, with errors clustered by country-year, the coefficient compares countries with one another. With country and year fixed effects it compares each country with itself over time, net of what all countries share in a year.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-macro
#| tbl-cap: "The centred national unemployment rate on the log-odds of naming each item, with the respondent characteristics of section 9.2 and the education × unemployment interaction of section 9.6, pooled and with country and year fixed effects; standard errors clustered by country-year. With the interaction in the model, each coefficient is the slope for the lowest education band."
inter |>
  datawizard::data_filter(term == "unemp_c") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(item = dplyr::if_else(item == "it9", "Unemployment", "Peace")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = item, Model = model, b = num(estimate, 4), SE = num(se, 4), z = num(z, 2), p = signif(p, 2)) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

For "Unemployment" the pooled comparison finds almost nothing, `r num(inter$estimate[inter$item == "it9" & inter$term == "unemp_c" & grepl("pooled", inter$model)], 3)` on the log-odds per point of unemployment; the within-country comparison finds `r num(inter$estimate[inter$item == "it9" & inter$term == "unemp_c" & grepl("fixed", inter$model)], 3)`, about a six per cent rise in the odds of naming unemployment for every point by which the national rate rises above its own average. Respondents in countries with high unemployment do not name unemployment more often than respondents in countries with low unemployment, but within any one country, respondents name it more often in years of rising unemployment than in years of falling unemployment. That is the between-and-within distinction of [section 5 of the statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-re), on one item and a binary outcome. For "Peace" the sign is negative under both designs and smaller within countries, which is the pattern that the scales built from these items inherit.

### 9.6 The education gap and the rate together {#sec-interaction}

The second part of the second hypothesis of the paper, H2b, states that the high-educated are more strongly affected by an economic downturn than the low-educated, and the [individual-level module](individual-level.qmd#sec-claim2) tests it on the scales with the unemployment rate as the measure of the downturn. On a single item the test is a product term, education band times the unemployment rate, and the table gives it under both designs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-interaction
#| tbl-cap: "Education × unemployment on the log-odds of naming each item, pooled and with fixed effects. Each interaction term is the difference between the unemployment slope of its band and that of the lowest band."
inter |>
  datawizard::data_filter(grepl(":", term)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(item = dplyr::if_else(item == "it9", "Unemployment", "Peace"),
         term = dplyr::if_else(grepl("high", term), "high × unemployment", "mid × unemployment")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Item = item, Model = model, Term = term, b = num(estimate, 4), SE = num(se, 4), z = num(z, 2), p = signif(p, 2)) |>
  tinytable::tt()
```

On these two items the interaction is absent: no product term reaches conventional significance under either design, and the fixed-effects estimates are at zero. The education gap in naming unemployment is large, and it neither widens nor narrows as the national rate moves. The hypothesis, however, is about the scales, which sum items with different prevalences and different movements, and the individual-level module reports what happens there, under the published design and under fixed effects, and under both rules for the respondents who named nothing. A result on a scale is a sum of results on items, not every one of which need show it, and that is the reason for looking one rung down the ladder before believing a coefficient one rung up.

### 9.7 A random intercept for the cluster {#sec-random}

The other treatment of the cluster is to give each country-year, and each country, its own intercept, drawn from a distribution whose spread the model estimates: the multilevel logit, which is the binary-outcome form of the models in [section 6 of the statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-multilevel). It is fitted here with glmmTMB, which took about twenty-five minutes on the four hundred thousand rows with the full covariate set; the older lme4 routine takes several times as long on the same model.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-random
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Multilevel logit for 'Unemployment': respondents in country-years in countries, with the respondent characteristics and the education × unemployment interaction. Fixed effects, selected terms, and the standard deviations of the two random intercepts."
if (is.null(rnd)) {
  cat("The random-intercept fit had not finished when this page was rendered; rerun fit_items_glm.R and re-render.") # r-style: keep – the message printed in place of the table
} else {
  rnd |>
    datawizard::data_filter(part == "random" | term %in% c("unemp_c", "edu3mid", "edu3high", "unemp_c:edu3mid", "unemp_c:edu3high", "sesunemployed")) |>
    datawizard::data_modify(term = dplyr::recode(term, unemp_c = "unemployment (centred)", edu3mid = "education: mid", edu3high = "education: high",
                         `unemp_c:edu3mid` = "mid × unemployment", `unemp_c:edu3high` = "high × unemployment",
                         sesunemployed = "unemployed")) |>
    dplyr::transmute(Part = part, Term = term, Estimate = num(estimate, 4),
              SE = dplyr::if_else(is.na(se), "", num(se, 4)), z = dplyr::if_else(is.na(z), "", num(z, 2))) |>
    tinytable::tt()
}
```

The variance components show how much of the variation in naming unemployment lies between countries and between country-years once the respondent characteristics are in the model. The fixed part of the model, the coefficients that are common to all country-years, gives much the same result as the models with country and year fixed effects in sections 9.5 and 9.6, with the cluster modelled instead of corrected for in the standard errors. In the lowest education band the log-odds of naming unemployment rise by `r num(rnd$estimate[rnd$term == "unemp_c"], 3)` per point of the national rate, against `r num(inter$estimate[inter$item == "it9" & inter$term == "unemp_c" & grepl("fixed", inter$model)], 3)` with the fixed effects, and neither education × unemployment term reaches conventional significance. Which of the two treatments to prefer is taken up in the multilevel section of the statistics module, and the answer does not depend on the link.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Try it

If you have built the respondent file, open `companion/_model-outputs/fit_items_glm.R` and change the two items to "Waste of money" (`it11`) and "Freedom to travel" (`it5`). Rerun it and read the education contrasts in section 9.2 and the within-country unemployment slope in section 9.5. Then replace the logit in one of the fits with a linear probability model, `feols()` instead of `feglm()`, and set its coefficient for the high-education band beside the average marginal effect of section 9.4. They should be close, and the reasons they are not identical are the two faults of the linear probability model that section 3 describes, a line without floor or ceiling and a variance that changes with the share.
:::

## 10. Where this leads {#sec-next}

In the housing-audit case the curve of the claim takes the models of sections 1 to 7 as they are, and the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) sets out which of them it keeps. In the cohabitation case the curve holds the logit of section 8 beside the complementary log-log model and the multinomial logit of the paper, and the [event-history module](event-history.qmd) treats the three as models of time to an event, with the life table and the competing risk of separation. In the EU-frames case a scale is a sum or a share of items like those of section 9, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-scoring) builds the three scoring rules from them. Once summed, the outcome is bounded and lumpy rather than binary, and the [bounded-outcomes section](stats-methods.qmd#sec-glm) of the statistics module fits the second member of the same family, the beta regression, to it. Both pages apply the same idea at two rungs of the ladder: a link that keeps predictions inside the range of values that the outcome can take and a conversion of the results back to the scale of the outcome.

## Sources {#sec-sources}

The models on this page are fitted with `lm()` and `glm()` from base R, with the HC2 standard error and the average marginal effect of the estimator of the course in `R/housing/_tools.R`, which `R/housing/check_parity.R` checks against `estimatr` and `marginaleffects`. The data are `cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv` and the curve `cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv`, both with codebooks; the analyses of the five Multi100 analysts are in `analysts5.csv`. @GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories treat logistic regression and its interpretation on the probability scale at length, and the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd#level-estimation) sets out which models, tests and scales the curve of the claim keeps.

The models of section 8 are fitted on `cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months.csv`, the person-months of the course rebuild of the unions from the public-use files of the NSFG, with `survey::svyglm()` [@Lumley2004AnalysisComplexSurvey] and the design of both surveys, as in the estimator of the case in `R/cohabitation/_tools.R`; the average predictions and comparisons come from marginaleffects, and the values of the curve from `spec_curve.csv` and `display_options.csv` beside it. @Allison1982DiscreteTimeMethodsEvent sets out the discrete-time models.

The models of section 9 were fitted with the fixest package for the pooled and fixed-effects logits and probits, the marginaleffects package for the average marginal effects, and glmmTMB for the random-intercept logit, on the respondent file described in the [respondent codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/eb_respondents_codebook.md); the script is `companion/_model-outputs/fit_items_glm.R`. The respondent characteristics follow the published coding of the original paper of the EU-frames case [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]. The ratio between logit and probit coefficients and the conversion to average marginal effects are textbook material; the quantitative-methods references on the [resources page](../resources.qmd) cover both.
